abstract: Large Language Models are revolutionizing applications, but their unique attack surfaces demand new security approaches. This talk introduces threat modeling for LLM applications using MITRE ATLAS, the first framework specifically designed for AI security. We'll explore how traditional threat modeling falls short when applied to generative AI systems and demonstrate practical techniques for identifying and mitigating LLM-specific vulnerabilities. Through real-world case studies and live demonstrations, attendees will learn to map attack paths, identify data leakage risks, and model prompt injection threats. You'll walk away with actionable methodologies to integrate into your development lifecycle, ensuring your LLM applications are secure by design. Whether you're building chatbots, code assistants, or enterprise AI solutions, this session provides the essential security foundation for the AI era.
elevator_pitch: Learn to threat model LLM applications using MITRE ATLAS framework. Practical security techniques for prompt injection, data leakage, and AI-specific vulnerabilities. Essential for developers building secure AI systems.
learning_objectives: Map LLM application architectures to MITRE ATLAS attack patterns and tactics
Identify and mitigate prompt injection and jailbreaking vulnerabilities
Conduct threat modeling exercises for generative AI use cases
Implement security controls throughout the LLM application development lifecycle
target_audience: Software developers, security engineers, AI/ML practitioners, DevOps teams, and security architects working with or planning to implement LLM applications. Intermediate to advanced security knowledge required.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of web application security concepts, familiarity with threat modeling principles, and working knowledge of LLM applications or AI systems. Attendees should understand concepts like prompt engineering and model APIs.

outline.content: Introduction: Why LLM Security is Different
outline.details: Setting the stage with LLM adoption statistics and unique security challenges. Contrasting traditional vs AI-specific attack surfaces.
Deep dive into ATLAS structure, tactics, techniques, and procedures. How it differs from ATT&CK. Live navigation of the framework.
Demonstration of prompt injection, jailbreaking, and data extraction attacks. Mapping these to ATLAS techniques with real examples.
Step-by-step threat modeling of an LLM-powered chatbot. Identifying assets, attack vectors, and mitigation strategies using ATLAS.
Implementing security controls, prompt design patterns, and monitoring approaches. Integration with SDLC and DevSecOps pipelines.
Audience questions, additional resources, and community engagement opportunities.

key_takeaways: Practical threat modeling methodology specifically for LLM applications using MITRE ATLAS
Concrete techniques for preventing prompt injection and jailbreaking attacks
Framework for identifying data leakage and privacy risks in generative AI systems
Actionable security controls that can be implemented immediately in development workflows
Resources and community connections for ongoing AI security learning
speaker_bio: Michael Moran is a senior security researcher specializing in AI and machine learning security. With over 8 years of experience in threat modeling and application security, he focuses on developing practical security frameworks for emerging technologies. Michael is a contributor to MITRE ATLAS and regularly speaks at security conferences on AI security topics. He currently works at [Company], where he leads AI security initiatives and helps organizations build secure machine learning systems.
previous_experience: Presented 'Threat Modeling Machine Learning Systems' at Black Hat USA 2023, 'AI Security Fundamentals' at RSA Conference 2024, and multiple sessions at OWASP chapters. Regular contributor to AI security research and MITRE ATLAS development. Background includes enterprise security consulting and academic research in adversarial machine learning.

live_demo.safety: All demonstrations will use safe, non-production data and include proper rate limiting
